description: Student team from MINT Exzellenzgymnasium taking on the "Lunar Landing Site Navigator" challenge. We will build a web tool that compares lunar south pole landing sites and dates by showing where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the horizon, so users can judge solar power and direct-to-Earth communication windows at a glance. Our skills: Python, data analysis, data visualization, machine learning and web development. We formed our team in person at school and are complete.
summary:
A mission to the Moon's south pole needs sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for contact. Near the pole the Sun and Earth stay low over the horizon, so the terrain around a site decides both, hour by hour. When a launch date slips, the planner needs the answer again.

Lunar Site Browser is a web app that answers this on one screen. Choose a landing site, mission dates and Earth stations: the app shows when the site is sunlit and when a station is geometrically visible, as one sentence, a timeline and a 3D view over the real terrain. It ranks 18 sourced south-pole sites, searches for better dates, and compares sites and periods. Every value is computed from NASA data and links to its source.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Pick a mission period, a science goal and the Earth stations to count. The app ranks 18 sourced south-pole sites and, for the chosen site, shows when it is sunlit and when at least one selected station is geometrically visible: as a sentence, a timeline and a 3D view with the Sun and Earth over the real terrain horizon. "Find better dates" searches the following 60 days for landing times that meet your thresholds. "If the mission slips" shows the same mission 1, 7 and 30 days later and at the nearest other site. Also included: a table of all sites for the mission dates or a whole year, a site assessment (slope, roughness, nearest permanent shadow, temperature), a first power estimate, custom sites anywhere south of 80° S (marked approximate), CSV export, a link that reproduces the view, and a flight plan for a saved mission.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Sun and Earth positions relative to the Moon come from NASA/JPL SPICE kernels (DE440), every 30 minutes from November 2026 to December 2030.

2. For each site, the highest terrain angle in 720 directions is computed from NASA's LOLA elevation model, out to 300 km.

3. The browser combines both: a moment is sunlit when any part of the Sun's disc is above the terrain. A station counts when it is above the terrain seen from the site and the Moon is above the station's minimum elevation.

The app is static files: no backend, no account, no cookies.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

On 27 Oct 2026 a first-time user asked three NASA tools for the Sun and Earth elevation at one south-pole site over two weeks. After about 14 minutes, one had given a wrong answer that looked right and two had given no number. Our app gives that answer in one screen, with its source, and repeats it for new dates or a nearby site when a schedule changes. It is meant for mission planners, students and anyone comparing landing sites.

TOOLS

Frontend: TypeScript, React, three.js, D3, Vite. Data pipeline: Python with SpiceyPy, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio and pyproj. Tests: vitest, Playwright, pytest. Hosting: Cloudflare. AI tools (Claude Code, Codex) wrote the code, the data pipeline and its tests; every session is logged with its errors and who checked it.

CREATIVITY

The app joins terrain, Earth stations and time into one answer sentence and one timeline instead of separate maps and tables. The 3D view shows the Sun and Earth over the actual horizon of the site. There is no weighted score: every ranked row shows the values it was ranked by. Each section explains itself in plain words for people who do not normally use such tools.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy: the app's Sun and Earth directions were compared with JPL Horizons at 72 body-site-time pairs; the largest elevation difference was 0.000043° against a tolerance of 0.05°. Honesty about limits: station contact is geometric line of sight, not a radio link (schedules, equipment, weather and link budget are not modelled). The 5° landing slope limit is our project criterion, not a NASA limit. Power is a first estimate, not a power budget. South polar region only, dates 1 Nov 2026 to 31 Dec 2030. Every dataset is cited with its licence.
